name: Kingdom of Prussia
summary: A north German kingdom built around Brandenburg and Prussia, famous for its army and efficient state; it rose to great-power status under Frederick the Great and united Germany in 1871.

location.value: Northern Germany and the Baltic; 348,779 km² in 1756.

terrain.value: Mostly flat, sandy land on the North European Plain, with lakes, marshes and few natural borders, which made it hard to defend.

climate.value: Temperate, with cold winters and warm summers, and more continental in the east.

resources.value: Grain and timber at first; later coal and iron in Silesia and the Ruhr, which powered industry in the 1800s.

disasters.value: The Seven Years’ War (1756–63) and the Napoleonic defeat of 1806 devastated the land and the treasury.

population.value: 4,500,000 in 1756, 5,800,000 in 1786 and 8,700,000 in 1797; the page does not give the figures for 1815 and 1871.

urbanisation.value: Berlin was the capital; Königsberg, Breslau and Stettin were other large towns. Industry made Berlin grow fast in the 1800s.

disease.value: Cholera epidemics struck in 1831 and again later in the 19th century, and smallpox was widespread before vaccination.

migration.value: Prussia welcomed Huguenot refugees (from 1685) and other Protestants, and later many people moved from the countryside to industrial cities.

economicBase.value: Prussia was poor in natural resources; the Zollverein customs union (1834) increased its influence over other German states. The page does not describe Junker estates.

tradeRoutes.value: The Zollverein customs union (1834) opened trade across the German states, with goods moving by river, canal and railway.

wealth.value: Poor land made rich by careful state finance.

moneyAndTax.value: The Prussian thaler was the main coin; taxes on land and a consumption tax in towns paid for the army.

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy until the 1848 revolutions, then semi-constitutional under the 1850 Constitution, which lasted to 1918; the lower house was elected by a three-class franchise and parliament had no control over the military.

keyRulers.value: Frederick I crowned himself “King in Prussia” on 18 January 1701; Frederick William I (from 1713) introduced conscription in 1717; Frederick the Great invaded Silesia in 1740; Wilhelm I became king in 1861 and emperor in 1871; Bismarck took office on 23 September 1862.

succession.value: The crown passed by hereditary succession in the Hohenzollern family, usually from father to eldest son.

institutions.value: A professional, disciplined civil service, a royal cabinet, and from 1848 a parliament with limited powers.

eliteConflict.value: The Junker landowning nobility dominated the army and state and clashed with liberals and the middle class, especially in 1848 and the 1860s constitutional crisis.

armyAndTech.value: A large standing army with strict training, the breech-loading needle gun, and a general staff that planned campaigns.

majorWars.value: Silesian invasion (1740) and the Seven Years’ War (1756–1763); defeat at Jena–Auerstedt in October 1806 and the Treaties of Tilsit (1807), which cost about half its territory; the Austro-Prussian War (1866); and the Franco-Prussian War (1870–1871).

territoryChange.value: Took Silesia (1742), parts of Poland (1772–95), Rhineland (1815).

alliancesRivals.value: Austria was the main rival for leadership of the German states; Russia, France and Britain shaped its alliances.

inventions.value: Few single inventions, but it led in military organisation, state schooling and the research university.

scienceEducation.value: Compulsory schooling and Wilhelm von Humboldt’s University of Berlin (1810), a model for the modern research university.

openness.value: Fairly open to religious minorities and foreign experts, though politically cautious and often censored.

communicationTransport.value: Railways spread from 1838 and the telegraph from the 1840s, joining the eastern and western provinces.

religion.value: Protestantism (Lutheran and Calvinist) was the majority, united in the Prussian Union church of 1817, and Catholics were a major minority (about 5.3 million of 14.1 million people in the 1830s).

languageWriting.value: German, written in Gothic and Latin scripts; Polish, Lithuanian and Danish were spoken in border regions.

artsArchitecture.value: The Brandenburg Gate (1791), Sanssouci Palace at Potsdam, and the neoclassical buildings of Karl Friedrich Schinkel.

socialStructure.value: The king and court, Junker nobility, middle-class officials and merchants, craftsmen, and peasants, many tied to estates until the 1807 reforms.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong ethos of duty, discipline and service to the state; over time it merged with German national feeling.

dailyLife.value: Most people lived in farming villages; garrison towns ran by the drum, and families paid for the army through taxes and conscription.

riseSignals.value: Frederick crowned himself “King in Prussia” on 18 January 1701; the location is not stated.

peakPeriod.value: Frederick the Great reigned 1740–1786. The infobox population rose from 2.2 million (1740) to 5.8 million (1786).

declineSignals.value: No decline as such: the kingdom was absorbed into the German Empire in 1871 and its monarchy ended in 1918.

outcome.value: Regained most of its pre-1806 territory at the Congress of Vienna. The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 at Versailles.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
